I have farmed these 15 mu in Quzhou for 42 years, and I know this land well. The soil here is loamy with decent natural fertility, but cotton pulls a lot of nutrients out, especially nitrogen once flowering and boll setting start. Last year I put down 20 kg of nitrogen per mu and got 350 kg of seed cotton per mu, but the late bolls ran small and the plants yellowed too early. This year I will push nitrogen to 22 kg per mu. I bought two extra 50-kg bags of urea from the dealer in town — that is an extra 240 yuan, but losing 30 kg of yield would cost me over 1,500 yuan at current prices. I would rather waste a little fertilizer than miss yield.

My base dressing is 50 kg per mu of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer at sowing, which gives me 7.5 kg each of N, P, and K. At budding I top-dress with 15 kg per mu of urea, and at peak flowering I add another 15 kg per mu of urea plus 10 kg per mu of potassium sulfate. The extension agent told me our local soils have been getting lower on potassium from years of cotton, and my own plots show the same. So my total nutrients come to about 22 kg nitrogen, 8 kg phosphorus, and 9 kg potassium per mu.

Irrigation comes from my well, but every run of the pump shows up on the electricity bill. I will irrigate four times: right after sowing for emergence, once at budding, once at flowering, and once at boll filling. That is what I did last year and what the other households around me with wells are doing. Five times would cost another 150 yuan in electricity for little extra benefit.

For pests, I plan five sprays. First spray targets aphids at seedling stage. Then two sprays around flowering for bollworm, and two more in late season for spider mites and whitefly. I looked online and the dealer confirmed that five is enough if you time them right. I am planting an improved Bt cotton variety — not the newest hybrid on the market, but one I have used for three years and know how it behaves. At 65 years old, I do not gamble on unknown seeds.

I use rotary tillage every spring. It loosens the topsoil for root growth and costs less than deep ploughing. For labor, my wife and I handle most of it, but at 15 mu I will hire two village workers for planting and another two for picking during peak season. The whole input budget — seed, fertilizer, pesticide, water, and hired labor — runs about 1,800 yuan per mu. If I hit 380 kg per mu and seed cotton holds at 7.5 yuan per kg, I clear about 1,000 yuan per mu after costs. That feeds my household of two and leaves something for savings.
